title: Development of microwave multiplexed readout for athermal phonon TES-based detectors
authors: Tran Tsan, Douglas A. Bennett, Daniel T. Becker, Rebecca Carney, Johnathon D. Gard, John A. B. Mates, Joel N. Ullom, Michael R. Williams, John C. Groh
abstract: Continued advancements in sub-eV calorimetric measurements are being enabled through the athermal phonon detection channel, with applications spanning a diverse array of fields, including low-mass dark matter searches, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, and quantum information science. While Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) have achieved the lowest thresholds to date, they face significant scalability bottlenecks due to the inherent constraints of conventional SQUID readout architectures. To address this limitation, we present an update on R&D to develop practical, highly multiplexed, microwave readout for athermal phonon TESs, which can enable a dramatic increase in both sensor count and target mass, with a focus on sub-GeV dark matter searches as a target application. This work leverages advances from highly scaled mm-wave, x-ray, and gamma-ray TES systems, adapting them to the unique needs of low-threshold rare event measurements. We quantify the basic readout functionality and noise level in our dilution refrigerator testbed and demonstrate operation of a variety of TES devices with saturation powers significantly lower than mm-wave and x-ray devices. We demonstrate proof-of-concept multiplexed readout of background event pulses, bound the readout's contribution to the parasitic TES background load to <1 fW, and discuss a cryogenic inline RF filtering scheme. These results demonstrate practical solutions to several of the key challenges that must be solved before a next-generation athermal phonon detector at scale is realized.
summary: This work details the development and testing of a microwave multiplexed readout system designed for next-generation athermal phonon TES detectors. By addressing the scalability bottlenecks of conventional readout methods, the authors demonstrated that the system can operate with extremely low background loads, paving the way for large-scale, ultra-sensitive detectors for rare event searches like dark matter detection.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a practical, highly multiplexed microwave readout system for athermal phonon Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) to overcome scalability limits for low-mass dark matter searches.
main_result: The authors demonstrated proof-of-concept multiplexed readout of background pulses, bounding the readout's parasitic background load to less than 1 fW, and established LTCC filters as viable inline microwave suppression components.
method: The research involves characterizing the readout functionality and noise level in a dilution refrigerator testbed using a Software-Defined Radio (SDR) based on an RFSoC, while testing various TES types.
model_or_system: The system utilizes athermal phonon TESs, superconducting sensors optimized for sub-eV energy detection. The readout employs a $\mu$mux chip architecture, adapted from higher-power detectors, operating at cryogenic temperatures ($\sim 10$ mK).
key_observables: Noise level (e.g., $34 	ext{ pA}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$), parasitic background load ($<1 	ext{ fW}$), and microwave filter rejection ($>20 	ext{ dB}$ at 10 mK).
important_parameters: TES Saturation Power ($P_{sat}$) in the fW range, operating temperature ($\sim 10 	ext{ mK}$), and the required scalability to $O(10^3)$ sensors.
main_assumptions: The primary challenge addressed is adapting multiplexing technology designed for higher $P_{sat}$ detectors to the extremely low $P_{sat}$ of athermal phonon TESs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the R&D setup (separated TES and $\mu$mux boxes), LTCC filter performance (cryogenic vs. room temperature transmission), and measurements of the detector's quality factor ($Q_i$) and noise spectra.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the microwave readout system, characterizes its noise and filtering capabilities, demonstrates its compatibility with low-$P_{sat}$ TESs, and discusses the feasibility of scaling the detector array.
why_interesting: While the focus is on detector technology rather than fundamental quantum dynamics, the use of superconducting circuits, cryogenic electronics, and quantum-limited noise measurements touches upon advanced topics in quantum measurement and low-noise physics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Schematic (top) and photographs (bottom) of our R&D setup. The basic µmux architecture follows [5], [9], with modifications for athermal phonon TES testing. The readout and detectors are housed in separate enclosures connected by twisted pair wires and 25-pin micro-D connectors. This separation permits optional inline filtering to reduce readout leakage into the detectors.

Fig. 3: Left: distribution of the resonator internal quality factors at 10 and 100 mK. The two distributions show that Qi does not change significantly at lower temperature. Right: power spectral density of the input current for different readout channels. The noise floor corresponds to ≈3.8 µΦ0/ √

Fig. 2: LTCC candidate filter performance. Left panel: cryo- genic transmission when tested without any radiation shield- ing. The stop band rejection is ≳30 dB, but with oscillations due to radiative coupling to the fridge’s mixing chamber can. Right panel: room temperature verification that the high- frequency oscillations can be removed with a simple radiation shield surrounding the filter component.

Fig. 4: Left: resistance vs. bias power relationships for the six TES devices tested, demonstrating that a wide range of saturation powers are feasible with our setup. The data points inside the superconducting transition regions are slightly con- taminated by the influence of residual background pulses; the jagged shapes are therefore not expected to reflect the true zero-frequency TES behavior. Right: examples of correlated pulses (indicative of athermal phonon bursts) detected with two QET channels on the same chip tuned into their super- conducting transition.

Fig. 5: Left: measured baseline readout signal shifts due to varying the tone power and phase. Right: change in power sensed by the TES, inferred through the nominal responsivity. The uncertainty is presently dominated by the high background pulse rate in our setup, as is evident from the significantly larger uncertainty on the current measurement while in the transition than above it.
